eras.name: Foundations
eras.background: Networked machines share no clock, and some crash or even lie. Researchers first defined event order, atomic commit and Byzantine faults. Then they proved no protocol can guarantee agreement when messages may be delayed without bound.

eras.name: Agreement protocols
eras.background: Paxos kept replicas consistent through crashes, and PBFT did the same through lying nodes. Paxos waited nearly a decade for journal publication, and turning it into a real system proved hard.

eras.name: Web scale
eras.background: Web companies ran on clusters of commodity machines where component failures were the norm. They kept consensus inside small coordination services, while many data stores relaxed consistency to stay available. Bitcoin carried agreement onto an open network of strangers.

eras.name: Strong consistency
eras.background: Coding around weak consistency proved costly for application developers. Spanner showed global transactions could work, and Raft made consensus easier to build in. Amazon S3 then made strong consistency its default.

nodes.label: Lamport clocks
nodes.problem: With no shared clock, machines cannot always tell which of two events came first.
nodes.idea: Order events by the messages between them, and have every replica apply commands in that order.
nodes.impact: Its state machine approach became the model that Paxos, Raft and PBFT implement.

nodes.label: Two-phase commit
nodes.problem: A transaction spanning several machines could end up committed on some and aborted on others.
nodes.idea: A coordinator collects every participant's vote, then tells all of them to commit or all to abort.
nodes.impact: Distributed databases still use it, though a failed coordinator can leave it blocked.

nodes.label: Byzantine agreement
nodes.problem: A faulty machine might not just stop, but send conflicting information to different peers.
nodes.idea: Pease, Shostak and Lamport show that without signed messages, agreement needs over two-thirds honest nodes.
nodes.impact: A later paper named these Byzantine faults, the model behind PBFT and blockchains.

nodes.label: FLP
nodes.idea: Fischer, Lynch and Paterson prove that without timing bounds, one crash can stall any agreement protocol.
nodes.impact: Practical protocols keep safety unconditional and use timeouts only to make progress.

from.why: Its protocols assumed messages arrive within a known time, which real networks do not promise.

nodes.label: Paxos
nodes.idea: Lamport's acceptors decide each value by majority; any two majorities overlap, so a chosen value survives.
nodes.impact: Most later consensus systems built on it, though it was notoriously hard to understand.

from.why: Supplied the state machine approach, but replicas still had to agree on each command despite crashes.
No protocol can guarantee progress, so safety must hold whatever the timing.

nodes.label: PBFT
nodes.idea: Castro and Liskov replicate a state machine that tolerates lying replicas on an asynchronous network.
nodes.impact: Made Byzantine tolerance practical, and permissioned blockchains later adopted BFT protocols.

from.why: Earlier Byzantine protocols assumed synchronous networks or were too slow to use.

nodes.label: CAP
nodes.idea: Fox and Brewer argue a replicated service can have at most two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance.
nodes.impact: Gilbert and Lynch proved it, and trading consistency for availability became an explicit choice.

from.why: Distributed transactions block during a network partition, which always-on web services cannot afford.

nodes.label: Chubby
nodes.idea: Google runs Paxos inside a small lock service that systems use to elect leaders and store metadata.
nodes.impact: GFS and Bigtable elect their masters through it, and Yahoo's ZooKeeper took the idea open source.

from.why: Teams rarely built their code around consensus, so leader election stayed ad hoc or manual.

nodes.label: Dynamo
nodes.idea: Amazon replicates with consistent hashing and sloppy quorums, and reconciles conflicting versions on read.
nodes.impact: Cassandra combined its replication design with Bigtable's data model.

from.why: Partitions force a choice between consistency and availability, and a shopping cart must stay writable.

nodes.label: Bitcoin
nodes.idea: Proof of work lets anyone join, and the longest proof-of-work chain fixes the order of transactions.
nodes.impact: Started public blockchains, which pulled Byzantine consensus back into wide use.

from.why: BFT protocols need every node to know the full membership, so strangers cannot simply join.

nodes.label: Spanner
nodes.idea: Paxos-replicated shards, two-phase commit across them, and TrueTime clocks with bounded error order transactions globally.
nodes.impact: Showed globally consistent transactions were practical; Google now offers it as Cloud Spanner.

from.why: Supplied atomic commit across shards, but its single coordinator hurt availability.
Without transactions, every application had to code around conflicts and partial updates itself.

nodes.label: Raft
nodes.idea: Ongaro and Ousterhout split consensus into leader election and log replication under one strong leader.
nodes.impact: Became the consensus inside etcd, Kubernetes' data store, and CockroachDB.

from.why: Paxos was hard to understand, and Chubby's builders found wide gaps between it and a real system.

nodes.label: S3 consistency
nodes.idea: Amazon made every S3 read return the latest write, via a cache coherence protocol checked with proofs.
nodes.impact: Strong consistency arrived at no extra cost or slowdown, removing customers' own workarounds.

from.why: Eventual consistency left applications to build their own checks for stale reads.

main.title: MIT 6.5840: Distributed Systems
main.why: Papers from MapReduce to PBFT, and labs that build MapReduce, Raft and a sharded key-value store on it. In English.
Machines share no clock, so Lamport clocks order events by the messages between them.

main.title: The Part-Time Parliament
main.why: The original Paxos paper, reaching consensus despite crashed and slow nodes, told as the story of a Greek parliament.

further.title: Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process

main.why: Paxos is hard to understand and build, so Raft splits consensus into leader election and log replication.

further.title: Paxos vs Raft: Have we reached consensus on distributed consensus?
Vive La Différence: Paxos vs. Viewstamped Replication vs. Zab

main.why: Rather than a Paxos library in every system, Google offers consensus as a lock service that GFS and Bigtable use to elect masters.
Instead of fixed lock primitives, ZooKeeper offers a small tree of files with watches, from which clients build locks and leader election.
Commodity disks fail constantly and files are huge, so GFS keeps metadata on one master and replicates large chunks across servers.
Structured data outgrew one database, so Bigtable splits sorted tables into tablets served across machines on GFS and Chubby.

main.title: Chain Replication for Supporting High Throughput and Availability
main.why: Strong consistency usually costs throughput, so chain replication passes writes down a chain of servers and serves reads from its tail.
In the cloud the network is the bottleneck, so Aurora ships only the redo log and lets the storage tier build pages.

main.title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook
main.why: Caching Facebook's reads in memcached brought stale sets and thundering herds, which leases and invalidations fix.

main.title: Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects
main.why: To define correctness for concurrent objects, linearizability requires each operation to appear to take effect instantly between its call and return.

further.title: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services
Diving Deep on S3 Consistency
further.why: S3 was eventually consistent, and making it strongly consistent without losing performance relied on proofs and model checking.

main.why: Amazon's cart must always accept writes, so Dynamo replicates with sloppy quorums and resolves conflicting versions on read.
DynamoDB shares Dynamo's name but not its design, running each partition as a Multi-Paxos group for predictable performance.
TrueTime bounds clock error, so transactions stay consistent across data centers.

main.title: Life beyond Distributed Transactions: an Apostate's Opinion
main.why: Distributed transactions do not scale, so large systems update one entity at a time and coordinate the rest with messages.

main.title: The Tail at Scale
main.why: With wide fan-out a few slow servers delay most requests, so services hedge requests and tolerate the tail.

further.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
further.why: Retries at every layer multiply load, so use backoff with jitter and a retry budget.

main.title: Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance
main.why: Earlier Byzantine protocols were too slow to use, so PBFT tolerates lying replicas with practical overhead.
